title: Original face
hookLine: what was your face before your parents were born (Gateless Gate 23)

lines: THE PASSPORT FACE. THE VIDEO-CALL FACE.
cards: Count your faces. The one in your passport photo. The one on video calls, slightly brighter than real life.
The face for your boss, the face for your oldest friend, the face you make at a baby. The one in the mirror at six in the morning, before you've decided who to be today. Which one is really you?
Zen has a question that goes further back than any of them, and it comes from a chase through the mountains. What was your face before your parents were born?

teach.b: Remember Huineng from two days ago, the poor man from the south who received the Fifth Patriarch's robe and bowl. The Gateless Gate, in case twenty-three, tells what happened next.
Huineng fled south with the robe, and some monks, furious that an outsider had it, chased him. The first to reach him, the story says, was a monk named Ming, once an army officer.
He caught up with Huineng in the mountains.
Huineng set the robe and bowl on a rock and said: this robe stands for faith; can it be taken by force? Take it. Ming tried to lift it.
It wouldn't move, as if it were a mountain. Shaking, Ming said: I came for the teaching, not the robe. Please teach me.

teach.h: DON'T THINK GOOD, DON'T THINK BAD.
teach.b: Huineng said: don't think good, don't think bad. Right now, at this very moment, what is your original face? Ming woke up on the spot.
He had come full of opinions: who deserved the robe, who was right, who was wrong. Huineng asks him to drop all of that and look at what's here before any of the labels.
Later Zen teachers put the same question another way, the version in today's title: what was your face before your father and mother were born? It isn't about biology or past lives.

It points at what you are before all the faces you've learned to wear, before good and bad, before your name. Teachers don't explain the answer. Like mu, like the flag, it's held and looked into until it looks back.

how: In Rinzai Zen 'original face' is often given as an early koan; students hold the question in sitting and daily life and bring their response to private interviews with the teacher.

o: how you looked as a baby, before life changed you
the face you'll be reborn with in your next life
what you are before every face you learned to wear

games.q: match each piece of the story.
p: set the robe and bowl on a rock
a monk who had been an army officer

s: the koan is asking about past lives
it points at what you are before every face and label.
in the Gateless Gate, Huineng asks it with 'don't think good, don't think bad'
the 'before your parents were born' wording is a later form of the same question.
Ming managed to carry the robe away
it wouldn't move, and he asked for the teaching instead.

games.q: you're Ming. you've caught up with Huineng, and the robe you chased won't budge from the rock. what do you do?
o: ask for the teaching instead of the robe.
go back and say you couldn't find him.
games.why: Ming asked to be taught, and Huineng asked him about his original face; the story says Ming woke up on the spot.

practice: If there's a mirror near you, look into it quietly; if not, close your eyes and feel your face from the inside, and let the expression you're wearing soften. Let the judgments that come, tired, older, fine, pass without arguing.
Then ask gently, without looking for an answer: what was my face before my parents were born?

wordCard.voice: Original face. What you are before good and bad, before every face you learned to wear: Huineng's question to Ming in the mountains.

orig.note: Chinese běnlái miànmù: original face, literally 'the face as it was from the start'.

carryVoice: Your line: before you were born. Under every face, the one you never had to learn. Day two hundred eighty-four, done.

sources.ref: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, Huineng and Huiming
